passage: The bus to the district town rattled past mustard fields, and Alka's cousin Rekha held up her phone. "Selfie? Wait, let me put the slimming filter." Alka covered the screen, laughing. "No filter. My face came all this way, it can be in the photo." A year ago Alka would have deleted every picture of herself. She had skipped meals, checked her reflection in every shop window and called herself ugly under her breath. When it got bad enough that she fainted at the tailoring shop, her mother took her to the doctor, and now she saw a counsellor in town every other Saturday. That was where they were going. At the bus stand Alka bought two plates of poha. "Lunch first. Always lunch first." Rekha frowned at her own face in the bus window. "I look huge today." "You look like someone who climbed to the hilltop temple faster than me this morning," Alka said.

Dear Minakshi,
You told me you've been avoiding the mirror and scrolling fitness pages all night. I get it more than you think. At nineteen, I used to hate every photo of myself.
A few things helped me. I muted every account that made me feel small. I started eating three proper meals, not skipping. I swam, and I started noticing what my body could do instead of how it looked: forty lengths, then sixty. When I caught myself saying something cruel about my body, I tried saying something kind instead, even if it felt silly.
But I'll be honest. When mine got serious, I needed a doctor and a counsellor. If it's taking over your day, please tell Masi, and we'll find someone. I'll come with you.
Vishal

passage:
Thanks for having me, Hafsa. So I'm Jomon, and for most of college I hated my body. I stood in front of the mirror listing everything wrong.
The change started on a trek in Munnar. At the top, legs shaking, I thought: this body just carried me up a mountain. It didn't care what I looked like.
After that I unfollowed every account that made me feel bad. I started eating regular meals instead of skipping and then bingeing. And I tried talking to myself like I'd talk to a friend. "You're tired, you did well today," instead of "You're disgusting."
But honestly, the biggest step was when I told my doctor how bad it had got. She referred me to a counsellor who specialises in this. The trek helped. The professional help is what really changed things.

qa.q: Where did Jomon's change start?
qa.a: On a trek in Munnar.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel at the top of the trek?
qa.a: Jomon felt amazed and grateful, realising the body had just carried them up a mountain.

qa.q: What steps from Jomon's story build a kinder relationship with the body?
qa.a: Valuing what the body can do, unfollowing harsh accounts, eating regular meals, speaking kindly to oneself, and getting a qualified professional when the struggle is serious.

qa.a: The doctor likely saw it as a brave and important step and responded by referring Jomon to a specialist counsellor.
